column4: God sends water from the sky, brings forth fruits as provision, and subjects ships and rivers; this supplies the cultivated gifts whose uncountability and human ingratitude 14:34 names.
By the measured water lodged in earth in 23:18, God produces palm and grape gardens with abundant fruit for people to eat.
The command to glorify the name of one's Lord gives the fitting response to the creating, measuring, guiding, and pasture-producing care of 87:2-4.
The first command is to read in the name of the Lord who created, identifying Rabb before the human's self-sufficient transgression in 96:6-7.
The command to read is repeated while the Lord is called the most generous, making 96:6-7 a rejection of acknowledged generosity.
God teaches the human what he did not know, completing the formative care that precedes the same human's transgression in 96:6.
God creates the human from a mixed drop for testing and gives hearing and sight, supplying the care to which 76:3 says gratitude or ingratitude answers.
Spouses, children, grandchildren, and good provision are given by God, yet people believe falsehood and deny God's favor; a whole history of nurture is cut from its giver.
God produces people and gives hearing, sight, and hearts, but little gratitude follows, directly pairing formative gifts with failed return.
Night is made for rest and day for sight, yet most people do not thank despite God's bounty to them.
God makes earth a settled place, forms people well, and provides good things, then identifies Himself as their Lord; ownership, fitting, and completed benefit meet.
Night and day are made for rest and seeking bounty so that people may give thanks, explicitly directing provision back toward gratitude.
Fresh and salt seas yield food and ornament, while ships cross so people may seek God's bounty and perhaps give thanks.
The subjected sea supplies food, ornaments, and travel for seeking God's bounty, and the sequence aims at gratitude.
Human creation begins from an extract of clay, opening a staged formation that parallels growth from prepared earth.
The human is then placed as a drop in a secure lodging, one distinct stage in gradual nurture.
Drop, clot, tissue, bones, flesh, and a new creation are formed in sequence, an especially full Quranic enactment of development حالًا فحالًا toward completion.
Creation from dust, drop, and clot proceeds through childhood, maturity, and old age, directly presenting the Lord's stage-by-stage formation.
People are created in their mothers through successive creations in three darknesses, then the ayah identifies this maker as Allah their Lord and sovereign.
Creation from a humble fluid begins a compact sequence of measured formation.
The fluid is placed in a secure lodging, showing protective nurture within the sequence.
The lodging holds it for a known term, adding duration and measure to formation.
God declares that He determined the process and is the best determiner, closing the staged womb scene with calibrated care.
God is said to have caused people to grow from earth as a growth, applying the section's plant image directly to divine nurture of humanity.
Abraham excludes the Lord of the worlds from the objects he calls enemies, separating the true Rabb from false claimants before listing His care.
The Lord of 26:77 is the One who created Abraham and guides him, the first stage of the care that defines true lordship.
He is the One who feeds and gives drink, making ordinary provision an ongoing act of the Rabb.
When Abraham is ill, the Lord heals him, extending nurture from provision to restoration.
The speaker asks whether any lord besides God should be sought when He is the Lord of everything, closely matching the source definition “the rabb of each thing is its owner.”
People are told to be rabbāniyyūn through teaching and studying scripture, a derivative of the named root that joins disciplined formation to divine learning.
Abraham tells his Lord that he settled descendants in an uncultivated valley, asks for fruit as provision, and states gratitude as the hoped-for response.
People are commanded to seek provision from God, worship Him, and thank Him, laying out giver, gift, and return in one ayah.
Believers are told to eat the good things God provided and thank Him if they worship Him, directly binding consumed provision to gratitude.
People must eat God's lawful good provision and thank God's favor, stating the response that kenud cuts off.
David's family is commanded to work in gratitude, and few servants are called truly grateful; gratitude is sustained action rather than mere possession of gifts.
People are told to remember when they were weak and afraid, then sheltered, strengthened, and given good provision so that they might thank.
Earlier peoples received abundant rain and flowing rivers but were destroyed for their sins and replaced, showing plentiful water as care that does not excuse refusal.
Seeking the Lord's forgiveness is followed by the promise of abundant rain and added strength, while turning away would sever that renewed relation.
At judgment the human is told to read his own record and is sufficient that day as reckoner against himself, a close parallel to self-witness in 100:7.
God has enumerated deeds that people forgot and will inform them of those deeds, then is called witness over everything; counting, forgetting, knowledge, and testimony converge.
Earth reports its news, turning the ground itself into a witness when hidden deeds are exposed.
Earth reports because its Lord inspired it, joining Rabb to the ground's testimony.
People emerge separately to be shown their deeds, specifying what the earth's report leads to.
Even an atom's weight of good is seen, so no return along the gift relation escapes disclosure.
Even an atom's weight of evil is seen, completing the exhaustive boundary of that disclosure.
The Creator knows what the human soul whispers and is nearer than the jugular vein, directly excluding escape from the Rabb's knowledge.
God knows every leaf that falls and every grain, حَبَّةٍ, in earth's darkness, joining the field's seed to complete knowledge of what is hidden.
A good word is likened to a good tree with a firm root and high branches, making stable relation visible as rooted growth.
The good tree gives fruit in every season by its Lord's permission, a verbal and conceptual parallel to the good land of 7:58.
God revives earth after its death immediately after warning against hardened hearts, inviting the responsive human to be read through receptive soil.
True righteousness includes giving wealth despite one's love for it, turning حُبّ of possession into an onward gift rather than kenud withholding.
The answer to what should be spent calls it خَيْر and directs it to relatives and vulnerable recipients, using the named word in an explicitly generous sense.
Whatever خَيْر people spend is for their own good and will be repaid fully, describing gift as a continuing rather than severed relation.
After helping others at the well, Moses tells his Lord that he is in need of whatever خَيْر He sends, recognizing good as a gift from its giver.
The rebuke after the two provision-tests says people do not honor the orphan, showing failed gratitude in treatment of another dependent.
They do not urge one another to feed the poor, so received provision does not continue outward.
They consume inheritance voraciously, preparing the charge of immense love of wealth in 89:20.
People will be questioned that day about enjoyed bounty, joining the loved gift to the knowing accountability it cannot escape.
The one who gives and is mindful embodies the continuing, generous response opposite the withholding kenud.
The one who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient combines the two central failures of the section: stopping the gift's flow and forgetting dependence.
Those summoned to spend from received wealth may withhold, but their stinginess harms themselves because God is self-sufficient and they are needy; turning away can bring replacement.
Believers are warned not to let wealth and children distract from remembrance of God, the precise boundary between loving gifts and forgetting their giver.
If family, acquired wealth, trade, and dwellings are more loved than God, people must await His command; حُبّ of gifts is measured against their giver.
After Qarun is swallowed, former admirers recognize that God expands and restricts provision and that His grace spared them, correcting their earlier fixation on the gift.
Turning away is associated with corrupting earth and severing kinship, a direct Quranic instance of refusing to maintain a relation.
The people of understanding fulfill God's covenant and do not break the compact, preserving the bond whose breakers appear in 13:25.
They join what God commands to be joined and fear their Lord, the explicit positive reversal of severing the giver's bond.
God is addressed as owner of dominion who gives and removes rule, while all ٱلْخَيْرُ is in His hand; ownership and good-as-gift meet.
When seated on a means of travel people are instructed to remember their Lord's favor, preserving the giver within enjoyment of the gift.
Despite those created means, the human assigns part of God's servants to Him and is called manifestly ungrateful.
The human sees that God created him from a drop yet becomes an open adversary, turning formative care into opposition.
The human offers a challenge about revived bones while forgetting his own creation, an exact case of forgetting prior nurture.
The answer points back to the One who produced creation the first time and knows every creation, restoring maker and knowledge together.
Towns that exulted in their livelihood were destroyed and left scarcely inhabited, showing provision enjoyed without a sustaining relation to its giver.
The Lord is declared ever watchful immediately before the human's mistaken readings of expanded and restricted provision in 89:15-16.
Usury given to grow through people's wealth does not grow with God, while alms seeking God's face are multiplied; apparent gain and true generous growth are reversed.
A bad word is like a bad tree uprooted from earth with no stability, the non-rooting counterpart to the fruitful tree of 14:24-25.
When the corrupt person turns away he destroys crops and livestock, actively undoing the nurturing field system rather than merely failing to yield.
A fruiting garden with rivers and every produce is struck by a fiery whirlwind when its owner is vulnerable, exposing the boundary of assumed possession.
The adornment on earth will be made barren ground, a temporal reversal from productive surface to land that yields nothing.
A cloud approaching the valleys is welcomed as rain, but is identified instead as the hastened punishment; the normally nurturing cloud carries the opposite outcome.
The wind destroys everything by its Lord's command, completing the reversal of the expected raincloud in 46:24.
Heaven's gates open with pouring water, but the abundant descent is judgment rather than plant-nurturing mercy.
Earth bursts with springs and the two waters meet for a decreed matter, a destructive counterpart to water collecting in receptive soil.
One who rejects false masters and believes in God grasps the firmest handhold that has no break, a positive boundary against the cut cord of gratitude.
Submitting oneself to God while doing good is described as grasping the firmest handhold, the maintained relation opposite kenud severance.
People are commanded to worship their Lord who created them and those before them, setting up the rain, fruit, and provision detailed in 2:22.
Sun, moon, night, and day are subjected for people, continuing the inventory of gifts that 14:34 says cannot be counted.
God places livelihoods on earth for people and for creatures they do not provide for, between measured growth in 15:19 and divine stores in 15:21.
A tree from Sinai produces oil and food, adding a particular cultivated yield to the watered gardens of 23:19.
After the rain-grown creatures of 31:10, God calls this His creation and challenges people to show what others created, restoring the maker behind the scene.
Water from the sky brings fruits of varied colors, a direct repetition of the cloud-to-yield part of the image.
God shows signs and sends provision from the sky, yet only one who turns back remembers, linking descent of provision to remembered giver.
God blesses earth and apportions its sustenance in measured days, presenting the field as fitted and provisioned rather than self-producing.
Earth is made a resting place with roads for guidance, preparing the measured water and revived land of 43:11.
Earth is spread, stabilized, and made to grow beautiful pairs before the blessed rain and grain of 50:9.
Earth is made manageable for people to traverse and eat from God's provision, joining prepared ground to received livelihood.
Between staged creation and the command to inspect food, the human is said not yet to have fulfilled what God commanded, naming failed response to the surrounding care.
The Lord creates the human from a clinging substance, specifying the humble beginning within 96:1's lordly creation.
God teaches by the pen, one concrete means of the instruction completed in 96:5.
God assembles the human in whatever form He wills, continuing the proportioning and balancing care of 82:7.
After the generous Lord's formation, people nevertheless deny judgment, showing care answered by denial.
Guardians are appointed over people, introducing the record of conduct that follows denial of judgment.
The guardians are noble writers, giving durable form to the testimony over conduct.
The recorders know what people do, adding informed testimony to the generous Lord's prior care.
The human once passed through a period when he was not a mentioned thing, framing the created dependence specified in 76:2.
Because the living God is Lord of the worlds, people are commanded to call on Him sincerely and praise Him after the provisions listed in 40:64.
God subjects the sea so ships may travel and people may seek His bounty and perhaps thank, another provision-to-gratitude formulation.
Night and day allow people to seek the Lord's bounty and calculate years and reckoning, linking provision with rightly directed counting.
God returns people to earth and will bring them out again, completing the human-as-growth image of 71:17.
Joseph tells one prisoner that he will pour wine for his rabb, using the named root in its secondary human-master sense.
Joseph asks the freed prisoner to mention him to his rabb, again using the root for a human master rather than the nurturing divine Lord.
Taking scholars and monks as lords beside God shows the obeyed-master sense of rabb redirected to improper claimants.
Pharaoh's claim “I am your highest lord” is the extreme false appropriation of ownership and mastery.
God speaks of completing His favor so that people may be guided, another direct use of completed bounty as an aim of care.
Completion of religion and favor is announced together, preserving the source section's definition of a benefit brought to completion.
Joseph's Lord will choose and teach him and complete His favor upon him and Jacob's family, making development itself a divine gift.
The Prophet's favor is completed and he is guided on a straight path, pairing completion with direction.
God shows lightning in fear and hope and raises heavy clouds, presenting the cloud before its water becomes either hoped-for provision or danger.
No recitation or deed is undertaken without God witnessing it, and not even an atom's weight escapes the Lord, grounding testimony in complete knowledge.
Whether what is within breasts is hidden or disclosed, God knows it, supporting the section's Lord informed of concealed inner contents.
Hearts are warned not to harden against God's remembrance immediately before 57:17 says He revives dead earth, making receptivity the bridge between person and soil.
A person who leaves خَيْر is instructed about a bequest; here the named word carries the wealth sense rather than the section's gift sense.
Affirming the finest promise distinguishes the giver in 92:5 from the denier paired with withholding in 92:9.
The giver is eased toward ease, the resulting path of the generous response in 92:5.
The self-sufficient withholder denies the finest promise, adding denial to the stopped flow of 92:8.
He is eased toward hardship, the consequence paired against the giver's ease in 92:7.
People are commanded to spend from what God provided before death makes them beg for delay to give, treating provision as something meant to continue onward.
Qarun's immense treasures make him exult, beginning the case of a recipient whose possession obscures its giver.
Those desiring the nearer life wish for Qarun's fortune, illustrating love fixed on the visible gift.
Those given knowledge say God's reward is better, placing a durable good against fascination with Qarun's wealth.
God causes earth to swallow Qarun and his dwelling, showing that possessed goods cannot protect their owner from the giver's command.
Justice, excellence, and giving to relatives are commanded immediately before covenant keeping in 16:91, joining maintained bonds to onward generosity.
The sequence of crop, water, and other provisions concludes by commanding glorification of the great Lord's name.
Many creatures cannot carry their provision, yet God provides for them and for people, emphasizing continuing dependence on the giver.
Abraham asks his Lord to make the city secure and provide its believing people with fruits, locating produce and safety in lordly provision.
Abraham is described as grateful for God's favors, chosen, and guided, a personal positive counterpart to kenud.
Joseph commands seven years of diligent sowing and keeping the grain in its ears, a concrete farmer-and-grain scene.
Seven hard years consume what was stored except a little, placing scarcity beside the cultivated abundance of 12:47.
A later year brings relief and pressing of produce, restoring yield after the scarcity of 12:48.
People are asked to look at how many noble pairs God caused earth to grow, a direct appeal to cultivated evidence.
The earth's diverse growth is called a sign, yet most people do not believe, connecting visible nurture with failed recognition.
The one who seeks the harvest of the Hereafter has that harvest increased, while the seeker of the world's harvest receives only some of it; field yield becomes a measure of chosen good.
Water springs from rock for the tribes, who are told to eat and drink God's provision without corrupting earth.
The sovereign creator owns heaven and earth, creates everything, and determines it precisely, combining ownership with measured formation.
A person who thought he would never return is corrected because his Lord was always seeing him, another form of inescapable lordly knowledge.
Joseph says “he is my rabb and made my lodging good”; whether rabb here denotes God or his human master is disputed, but either reading joins benefaction to refusal to betray the relation.
The ayah literally places an extended means or rope beside an act of cutting it; the rhetorical context is different, so this is only an uncertain visual echo of the section's cut cord.
Mountains are left as a level plain, recalling the source dictionary's level ground, though this eschatological surface is not cultivated soil.
No crookedness or unevenness is seen in that plain, a precise shape parallel to the level-soil definition but in a different context.

Wives are called a tilth, bringing marital relation and soil into one metaphor; the link to the source's separate “woman who does not maintain connection” and “non-growing earth” senses remains indirect.

The Lord does not destroy towns unjustly while their people are reformers; this indirectly places Rabb beside iṣlāḥ, one of the source dictionary's lordly senses, without identifying the two roles outright.
